# Stopping Effects and Collective Flow in U+U Collisions: Insights from the ART1.0 Transport Model

## Introduction and Methodology

A Relativistic Transport Model, specifically the ART1.0 (A Relativistic Transport) framework, was employed to investigate nuclear stopping phenomena in uranium-uranium (U+U) collisions. The study focused on two extreme geometric orientations of the highly deformed uranium nuclei: tip-tip configurations, where the elongated axes of the colliding nuclei are aligned along the beam direction, and body-body configurations, where the nuclei collide side-on. These simulations were performed at a beam kinetic energy of 520 MeV per nucleon, a regime relevant to intermediate-energy heavy-ion physics and particularly significant given upcoming experimental capabilities in this energy range.

## Nuclear Stopping in Central Collisions

The simulation results demonstrate that central collisions in both the tip-tip and body-body orientations achieve a high degree of nuclear stopping. This complete stopping effect leads to the formation of a substantial, hot, and dense nuclear matter bulk. The strongly deformed geometry of the uranium nuclei plays a critical role in this process: because uranium nuclei possess a pronounced quadrupole deformation, central collisions—regardless of orientation—generate an overlap region with sufficient volume and a sufficiently long-lived reaction zone to allow the compressed nuclear matter to reach conditions approaching local thermal and chemical equilibrium. This makes U+U collisions particularly advantageous compared to spherical nuclei of similar mass, as the deformation enhances the achievable energy density and interaction volume under specific orientation-controlled geometries.

## Sideward Flow Observations

A notable distinction between the two collision orientations emerges when examining the nucleon sideward (directed) flow. The simulations reveal that at small normalized impact parameters (b/b_max < 0.5), the sideward flow generated in tip-tip collisions is approximately three times larger in magnitude than that observed in body-body collisions. This substantial difference underscores how the initial spatial configuration of the deformed nuclei strongly influences the subsequent dynamical evolution of the collision, translating orientation-dependent geometric effects into measurably distinct flow signatures.

## Elliptic Flow as an Orientation-Sensitive Probe

Perhaps the most striking result concerns the nucleon elliptic flow (v2), which serves as a sensitive probe of the collision geometry and the underlying nuclear equation of state (EoS). The simulations show that body-body central collisions produce the largest negative elliptic flow, reaching v2 = -12%, indicative of strong out-of-plane emission consistent with squeeze-out effects in a highly compressed, elongated interaction zone. In stark contrast, tip-tip central collisions yield essentially zero elliptic flow. This pronounced contrast between the two orientations highlights the exceptional sensitivity of the elliptic flow observable to both the initial collision geometry and the properties of the nuclear EoS, making it a powerful diagnostic tool for probing the equation of state under controlled, orientation-selected conditions.

## Future Experimental Prospects

These theoretical predictions gain particular significance in light of the forthcoming Cooling Storage Ring (CSR) External Target Facility (ETF) in Lanzhou, China. This next-generation facility will be capable of delivering uranium beams at kinetic energies up to 520 MeV per nucleon, precisely matching the energy regime explored in the present simulations. The availability of such high-intensity, high-energy uranium beams will enable direct experimental tests of the predicted orientation-dependent flow signatures. As such, the CSR-ETF is poised to play a pivotal role in advancing our empirical understanding of the nuclear equation of state, offering an unprecedented opportunity to validate transport model predictions and refine our knowledge of dense nuclear matter properties through carefully designed U+U collision experiments.

# Stopping and Flow Effects in Deformed Uranium-Uranium Collisions: An ART1.0 Transport Model Study

## Introduction

The study of heavy-ion collisions provides a unique experimental window into the properties of nuclear matter under extreme conditions of density, temperature, and pressure. Among the various probes available to nuclear physicists, collisions involving deformed nuclei—particularly uranium (U)—offer a distinctive advantage due to their non-spherical shape, which allows experimentalists to select specific collision geometries by controlling the relative orientation of the colliding nuclei. This capability opens new avenues for investigating the nuclear equation of state (EOS) and the dynamics of compressed nuclear matter formation.

In this work, we employ A Relativistic Transport model (ART1.0) to simulate uranium-uranium (U+U) collisions at a beam energy of 520 MeV per nucleon, a regime relevant to the upcoming experimental capabilities at the Cooler Storage Ring-External Target Facility (CSR-ETF) in Lanzhou, China. Our primary objective is to systematically investigate how the two extreme orientations of the deformed uranium nuclei—the tip-tip configuration, where the long axes of both nuclei align with the beam direction, and the body-body configuration, where the long axes are oriented perpendicular to the beam—influence key observables related to nuclear stopping and collective flow.

## Motivation and Physical Background

Uranium nuclei possess a prolate deformation, characterized by an elongated shape along one axis. When two such nuclei collide, the geometrical overlap and the resulting participant zone depend critically on their mutual orientation at the moment of impact. In the tip-tip configuration, the nuclei approach each other along their long axes, resulting in a highly elongated and compact overlap region. Conversely, in the body-body configuration, the nuclei collide side-on, leading to a broader, more extended interaction zone in the transverse plane.

These distinct geometries are expected to produce markedly different conditions in the hot, dense nuclear matter formed during the collision, affecting both the degree of stopping (i.e., the conversion of longitudinal kinetic energy into thermal and transverse degrees of freedom) and the subsequent collective flow patterns that develop as the system expands and freezes out. Understanding these differences is essential not only for characterizing the properties of the created matter but also for extracting reliable constraints on the nuclear EOS, which governs the pressure-density relationship of nuclear matter at supra-normal densities.

## Simulation Setup

The ART1.0 transport model, a well-established microscopic framework for simulating relativistic heavy-ion collisions, was employed to model the dynamical evolution of U+U collisions at 520 MeV/nucleon. This model incorporates the relevant hadronic degrees of freedom, mean-field interactions, and two-body collision processes necessary to capture the essential physics of compression, thermalization, and expansion in heavy-ion reactions at this energy scale.

Two extreme orientation configurations were simulated: the tip-tip orientation and the body-body orientation, both at central or near-central impact parameters to maximize the geometric effects associated with nuclear deformation. The simulations tracked the space-time evolution of the collision system, allowing for the extraction of key observables including the degree of nuclear stopping, the lifetime and size of the hot, dense matter formed, and various flow coefficients characterizing the momentum-space anisotropies of the emitted particles.

## Key Findings

### Stopping and Hot Dense Matter Formation

The simulations reveal that both the tip-tip and body-body orientations achieve a high degree of nuclear stopping at this beam energy. In both cases, the collision results in the formation of a large, long-lived region of hot, dense nuclear matter, indicating that the incident kinetic energy is efficiently converted into thermal excitation and compression regardless of the specific orientation. This robust stopping behavior confirms that 520 MeV/nucleon U+U collisions are well-suited for probing the properties of compressed nuclear matter, as substantial baryon density and thermalization are achieved in both extreme geometrical configurations.

### Sideward Flow (Directed Flow)

Despite the similarity in stopping power, the two orientations exhibit striking differences in their collective flow observables. The sideward (directed) flow, which characterizes the in-plane transverse momentum development as a function of rapidity, is found to be nearly three times larger in tip-tip collisions compared to body-body collisions. This substantial enhancement in the tip-tip configuration reflects the more elongated and asymmetric compression zone created when the nuclei collide along their long axes, leading to stronger pressure gradients that drive enhanced directed collective motion.

### Elliptic Flow

Perhaps the most striking distinction between the two orientations emerges in the elliptic flow observable (v2), which quantifies the azimuthal anisotropy of particle emission in the plane transverse to the beam direction. The body-body configuration produces a distinctly negative elliptic flow, with v2 approximately equal to -12%, signaling a pronounced out-of-plane (squeeze-out) emission pattern. In stark contrast, the tip-tip configuration yields an elliptic flow value close to zero, indicating an essentially isotropic transverse emission pattern with no preferential in-plane or out-of-plane enhancement.

This dramatic difference in v2 between the two orientations arises directly from the distinct initial geometries: the body-body configuration creates a broader, disk-like overlap region in the transverse plane, naturally leading to squeeze-out flow as the compressed matter expands preferentially out of the reaction plane, whereas the more compact, elongated geometry of the tip-tip configuration does not favor such an anisotropic expansion pattern.

## Discussion and Implications

These findings demonstrate that while the overall degree of nuclear stopping is similar between the tip-tip and body-body orientations, the collective flow observables—particularly the sideward flow and elliptic flow—are highly sensitive to the specific collision geometry dictated by nuclear deformation. This sensitivity provides a powerful and complementary set of experimental observables for probing the nuclear equation of state.

Specifically, the pronounced difference in elliptic flow between the two orientations (near-zero for tip-tip versus strongly negative for body-body) offers a particularly clean experimental signature that can be exploited to disentangle the effects of nuclear geometry from those of the underlying nuclear interactions. Similarly, the significant enhancement of sideward flow in the tip-tip configuration relative to body-body collisions provides an additional independent handle on the dynamics of compressed nuclear matter formation.

## Relevance to CSR-ETF Facility

These results carry direct relevance for the experimental program planned at the CSR-ETF facility in Lanzhou, China, which will provide a unique opportunity to study heavy-ion collisions at beam energies in this regime with high precision and statistics. The ability to experimentally select and control the orientation of deformed uranium nuclei—through techniques such as event-by-event characterization of the initial collision geometry—will allow researchers to directly access the distinct physical regimes identified in this simulation study.

By comparing experimental measurements of sideward and elliptic flow in U+U collisions across different orientations with the predictions presented here, it will be possible to place stringent constraints on the nuclear equation of state at the densities and temperatures achieved in these collisions. The complementary nature of the tip-tip and body-body configurations—providing contrasting yet consistent probes of the same underlying physics—significantly enhances the discriminating power of such measurements.

## Conclusion

This study demonstrates, through detailed ART1.0 transport model simulations, that extreme orientations of deformed uranium nuclei in U+U collisions at 520 MeV/nucleon lead to significantly different collective flow signatures, despite both configurations achieving comparable levels of nuclear stopping and hot, dense matter formation. The nearly threefold enhancement of sideward flow in tip-tip collisions, combined with the striking contrast in elliptic flow (-12% in body-body versus approximately zero in tip-tip configurations), establishes these two extreme geometries as sensitive and complementary experimental probes. These findings provide valuable theoretical guidance for the upcoming experimental program at the CSR-ETF facility in Lanzhou, where such orientation-dependent studies of deformed nucleus collisions promise to substantially advance our understanding of the nuclear equation of state under extreme conditions.

# Relativistic Transport Models: Bridging Microscopic Dynamics and Macroscopic Observables

Relativistic transport models represent a fundamental theoretical framework used to describe the dynamical evolution of many-body systems under conditions where particle velocities approach the speed of light. These models find extensive application in nuclear physics, particularly in the study of heavy-ion collisions at relativistic energies, where they serve as essential tools for interpreting experimental data from facilities such as RHIC, LHC, FAIR, and NICA.

## Theoretical Foundations

At their core, relativistic transport models are built upon covariant kinetic equations that generalize the classical Boltzmann equation to account for relativistic kinematics and field theory. The most widely used formulations include the Relativistic Boltzmann-Uehling-Uhlenbeck (RBUU) equation and various quantum molecular dynamics approaches such as UrQMD (Ultra-relativistic Quantum Molecular Dynamics) and AMPT (A Multi-Phase Transport model). These frameworks describe the time evolution of phase-space distribution functions for various particle species, incorporating both mean-field potentials and collision terms.

The transport equation typically takes the form:

$$\partial_t f + \vec{v} \cdot \nabla_r f + \vec{F} \cdot \nabla_p f = C[f]$$

where f represents the phase-space distribution function, F denotes the mean-field force, and C[f] represents the collision integral accounting for two-body and multi-particle interactions.

## Key Physical Ingredients

Relativistic transport models incorporate several crucial physical elements:

**Mean-field potentials**: These describe the average interaction experienced by particles due to the surrounding medium, often derived from relativistic mean-field theories such as the Walecka model or density-dependent hadronic field theories.

**Collision terms**: These account for binary and higher-order collisions between particles, including elastic and inelastic scattering processes, particle production, and absorption.

**In-medium effects**: Modifications to particle properties (masses, widths, cross-sections) due to the surrounding nuclear medium are essential for accurately capturing the physics of dense, hot matter.

**Equation of state**: The models must incorporate a realistic equation of state that governs the relationship between pressure, energy density, and baryon density under extreme conditions.

## Applications

Relativistic transport models have proven invaluable for:

1. **Heavy-ion collision studies**: Simulating the entire collision process from initial impact through thermalization, expansion, and freeze-out, allowing researchers to extract information about the nuclear equation of state and properties of the quark-gluon plasma.

2. **Symmetry energy constraints**: Providing critical constraints on the density dependence of the nuclear symmetry energy, which has direct implications for neutron star physics and astrophysical phenomena.

3. **Particle production mechanisms**: Understanding the production of exotic particles, strange matter, and rare probes that carry information about the early, hot stages of collisions.

4. **Transport coefficients**: Extracting fundamental properties such as shear viscosity, bulk viscosity, and thermal conductivity of strongly interacting matter.

## Challenges and Future Directions

Despite their success, relativistic transport models face ongoing challenges, including the treatment of quantum effects, proper incorporation of chiral symmetry restoration, and the transition between hadronic and partonic degrees of freedom. Comparative studies between different transport codes, such as those conducted through the Transport Model Evaluation Project (TMEP), continue to refine our understanding of systematic uncertainties and improve the reliability of theoretical predictions.

As computational capabilities advance and experimental precision increases, relativistic transport models continue to evolve, incorporating more sophisticated treatments of quantum statistics, non-equilibrium dynamics, and the rich phase structure of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) matter under extreme conditions.

# Deformed Uranium-Uranium Collisions: Tip-Tip vs. Body-Body Orientations at Intermediate Energies

## Overview

Uranium nuclei possess a prolate (rugby-ball-like) deformation that makes U+U collisions uniquely sensitive to nuclear geometry effects not present in spherical-nucleus collisions (e.g., Au+Au). By selecting specific orientations—**tip-tip** (long axes aligned with beam direction) and **body-body** (long axes perpendicular to beam, sides facing each other)—simulations can isolate how initial-state geometry translates into final-state flow observables, providing a novel handle on the nuclear equation of state (EoS) at intermediate beam energies (roughly few hundred MeV/nucleon to a few GeV/nucleon, relevant to transport model studies like UrQMD, IQMD, or AMPT).

## Key Physics Results

### 1. **Initial Overlap Geometry and Participant-Spectator Configuration**
- **Tip-tip collisions**: Produce a highly elongated, small-eccentricity overlap zone along the beam axis, leading to a longer effective path length for nucleons traversing the collision zone, but a smaller transverse size.
- **Body-body collisions**: Generate a larger transverse overlap area with higher initial eccentricity, resembling (but exceeding) the elliptical geometry seen in mid-central spherical-nucleus collisions.

This difference in initial spatial geometry directly seeds different pressure gradients, which the EoS then converts into momentum-space anisotropies (flow).

### 2. **Directed Flow (v₁)**
- **Body-body configurations** show enhanced directed flow slopes (dv₁/dy near midrapidity) due to the larger transverse pressure gradients pushing participant nucleons preferentially in-plane.
- **Tip-tip configurations** exhibit suppressed v₁ because the elongated geometry reduces the transverse pressure buildup, weakening the sideward deflection signal.
- The **splitting between tip-tip and body-body v₁** is a direct fingerprint of the initial geometry and is highly sensitive to the compressibility (stiffness) of the EoS—stiffer EoS amplifies the difference.

### 3. **Elliptic Flow (v₂)**
- **Body-body** collisions yield significantly **larger v₂** than tip-tip, consistent with the larger initial spatial eccentricity converting more efficiently into momentum anisotropy under pressure-driven expansion.
- **Tip-tip** collisions show v₂ suppressed toward near-zero or even slightly negative values at certain rapidities, since the nearly circular (in transverse plane) overlap minimizes eccentricity-driven squeeze-out.
- The **v₂ splitting ratio between orientations** serves as a sensitive differential observable: unlike v₂ in Au+Au (which convolves impact parameter and fluctuation effects), the U+U orientation-selected v₂ isolates the *geometry-to-momentum* conversion efficiency, which is EoS-dependent (particularly sensitive to the pressure buildup during the compression stage).

### 4. **Squeeze-Out and Spectator Shadowing Effects**
- In **tip-tip** collisions, reduced transverse spectator shadowing allows nucleons/fragments to escape more isotropically, weakening out-of-plane squeeze-out flow.
- In **body-body** collisions, spectator matter more strongly shadows the in-plane direction, enhancing the out-of-plane squeeze-out component of elliptic flow (negative v₂ at high transverse momentum), a signature historically used to constrain the high-density EoS in Au+Au studies.

### 5. **Sensitivity to Nuclear EoS Stiffness**
- Simulations run with **soft vs. stiff EoS** parametrizations show that the tip-tip/body-body flow differences (v₁ and v₂ splittings) are **amplified under a stiffer EoS**, since stronger pressure gradients more efficiently translate initial geometric differences into momentum-space flow.
- This makes orientation-selected U+U collisions a potentially powerful **differential probe**: rather than relying on absolute flow magnitudes (which depend on many nuisance parameters like impact parameter, nucleon-nucleon cross-sections, and mean-field parameters), the **ratio or difference between tip-tip and body-body flow observables** offers a cleaner constraint on EoS stiffness, partially canceling out common systematic uncertainties.

### 6. **Multiplicity and Stopping**
- Body-body collisions generally show higher charged-particle multiplicities and greater nucleon stopping (more complete thermalization) due to larger overlap volume and increased number of binary collisions in the transverse-facing geometry.
- Tip-tip collisions show reduced stopping, with more nucleons retaining longitudinal momentum, consistent with a more transparent, elongated collision geometry.

## Relevance to Nuclear EoS Studies

The central significance of this line of study is that **orientation control acts as a "geometric knob"** unavailable in spherical systems: by comparing flow observables between tip-tip and body-body events (selected either by simulation or experimentally via event-shape/multiplicity discrimination), one can:

1. **Disentangle initial-state geometry from EoS-driven dynamics** — the same colliding system, same beam energy, but two very different initial eccentricities, allows a controlled differential measurement.
2. **Reduce systematic uncertainties** relative to single-configuration analyses, since common initial-state uncertainties (nucleon-nucleon cross sections, general transport parameters) largely cancel in the ratio/difference of tip-tip vs. body-body observables.
3. **Provide new constraints on symmetric and possibly asymmetric nuclear matter EoS** at the supra-saturation densities reached in intermediate-energy heavy-ion collisions, complementing existing constraints from Au+Au flow, kaon production, and neutron star observations (multi-messenger EoS constraints).

## Summary Statement

Simulations of tip-tip and body-body U+U collisions at intermediate energies reveal that the extreme deformation of uranium translates into markedly different initial eccentricities, driving significant splittings in directed and elliptic flow, spectator shadowing, and stopping power between the two orientations. These orientation-dependent flow observables are shown to be sensitive to the underlying nuclear EoS stiffness, and their **differential (rather than absolute) comparison** offers a promising, largely systematic-uncertainty-reduced pathway to further constrain the nuclear equation of state at high baryon densities.

# Research Summary: Nucleon Collective Flow in Orientation-Selected U+U Collisions

## Background and Motivation

The prolate deformation of ²³⁸U nuclei allows for geometrically distinct collision configurations—tip-tip (long axes aligned with beam) and body-body (long axes perpendicular to beam)—that are not accessible with spherical nuclei. These configurations produce markedly different initial overlap geometries and energy densities at fixed centrality, offering a novel lever arm for probing the nuclear equation of state (EOS) through collective flow observables.

## Methodology

Using a transport model (e.g., UrQMD/AMPT-type framework) with realistic deformed Woods-Saxon nucleon distributions, tip-tip and body-body U+U collisions were simulated at fixed impact parameter and beam energy. Nucleon sideward flow (directed flow, v₁) and elliptic flow (v₂) were extracted as functions of rapidity and transverse momentum, comparing results obtained with soft versus stiff nuclear EOS parameterizations (varying incompressibility K and momentum-dependent interactions).

## Key Findings

**Sideward Flow:** Tip-tip collisions, characterized by a more compact, elongated overlap along the beam axis, generate enhanced longitudinal compression and consequently stronger sideward (directed) flow compared to body-body configurations. The tip-tip geometry more closely resembles central spherical-nucleus collisions in its compression dynamics, amplifying the pressure gradients that drive v₁.

**Elliptic Flow:** Body-body collisions produce a pronounced almond-shaped transverse overlap region, analogous to peripheral spherical collisions, resulting in significantly larger elliptic flow due to stronger spatial eccentricity converting into momentum-space anisotropy. Tip-tip collisions, being more axially symmetric in the transverse plane, yield substantially suppressed v₂.

**EOS Sensitivity:** Both flow observables in each configuration respond differently to the stiffness of the EOS:
- A **stiffer EOS** enhances sideward flow magnitude and speeds up its development, with tip-tip configurations showing the largest EOS-driven splitting due to greater compression.
- **Elliptic flow** in body-body events is more sensitive to early-stage pressure buildup, with stiffer EOS accelerating the eccentricity-to-momentum conversion and increasing v₂ at early times, while softer EOS delays and dampens this conversion.

The **difference between tip-tip and body-body flow signals** (Δv₁, Δv₂) is shown to scale with EOS stiffness, providing a differential, geometry-controlled observable that reduces sensitivity to other systematic uncertainties (e.g., initial-state fluctuations) that typically obscure EOS extraction in standard spherical-nucleus collisions.

## Conclusions

The tip-tip/body-body dichotomy in U+U collisions offers a powerful, complementary method for constraining the nuclear EOS at high baryon density. Because both configurations share the same nuclear species and beam energy, comparing their flow observables isolates geometry-driven effects and enhances discriminating power between soft and stiff EOS scenarios beyond what is achievable with centrality selection alone in spherical systems. These results motivate dedicated experimental orientation-selection techniques (e.g., using multiplicity or spectator asymmetry) at RHIC/LHC energies to fully exploit this diagnostic channel.

counterfactuals.output:
# Abstract

We present a theoretical study of nuclear stopping and collective flow observables in ultra-central and extreme-geometry ²³⁸U+²³⁸U collisions at a beam energy of 520 MeV/nucleon, motivated by the physics program planned for the External Target Facility at the Cooler Storage Ring (CSR-ETF) in Lanzhou. Owing to its pronounced prolate deformation, uranium offers a unique opportunity to select distinct initial-state geometries—body-body (tip-tip) and side-side (body-body perpendicular) configurations—by exploiting orientation-dependent observables, thereby providing tighter constraints on the nuclear equation of state and in-medium nucleon-nucleon cross sections than achievable with spherical nuclei.

Using a transport model framework (e.g., an isospin- and momentum-dependent Boltzmann-Uehling-Uhlenbeck-type approach), we simulate collisions across a range of impact parameters and relative orientations of the deformed uranium nuclei, systematically varying the nuclear symmetry energy, incompressibility, and momentum dependence of the mean-field potential. We quantify the degree of nuclear stopping via the rapidity distribution width and the ratio of transverse-to-longitudinal momentum (the "stopping" or vartheta observable), demonstrating that tip-tip configurations approach more complete stopping due to larger overlap along the beam axis, while side-side collisions retain larger residual longitudinal motion.

We further compute directed (v₁) and elliptic (v₂) flow coefficients as functions of rapidity, transverse momentum, and centrality, showing that the deformed geometry induces sizable modifications in the flow anisotropies compared to spherical-nucleus collisions at equivalent centrality classes. The sign and magnitude of v₂ are found to be sensitive both to the orientation-selected initial eccentricity and to the stiffness of the equation of state at supra-saturation densities reached in these collisions (up to ~2-3 times normal nuclear matter density at this beam energy).

Our results indicate that combining stopping-power measurements with flow observables in orientation-selected U+U collisions at CSR-ETF energies can serve as a sensitive differential probe of the high-density equation of state, complementing existing constraints from RHIC and lower-energy heavy-ion facilities. We provide quantitative predictions for experimentally accessible observables—including the stopping parameter, v₁ and v₂ as functions of centrality and pseudorapidity—to guide future data analysis and detector design considerations for the CSR-ETF program, establishing baseline expectations against which upcoming measurements can be compared to extract equation-of-state parameters in the previously underexplored energy regime of a few hundred MeV per nucleon.
